did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job compares human life to a period of service or appointed labor, and likens it to the days of a hired worker waiting for his work to end.
Did you know? This verse presents two images of a laboring person: a slave longing for shade so he can rest, and a hired worker hoping to receive his wages after finishing his work.
Did you know? Job describes severe sleeplessness: even after lying down, he asks when he will get up and portrays the night as a succession of restless hours until morning.
Did you know? The description of Job’s body emphasizes the severity of his suffering through images of worms, clods of dirt, and skin that cracks and festers.
Did you know? Job compares the speed at which his days pass to the movement of a weaver’s shuttle, which moves quickly across the loom, emphasizing that his days pass without hope.
Did you know? Job describes his life as a passing breath and asks that it be remembered how short his life is, before his eyes cease to see good.
Did you know? The vanishing cloud serves as an image of human disappearance: just as a cloud passes away and is gone, so the one who goes down to Sheol does not return.
Did you know? Job declares that he will not remain silent but will speak out of his anguished spirit and express the bitterness of his soul; this is a direct expression of his protest and distress.

Did you know? In asking, “Am I the sea, or a sea monster?” Job uses a rhetorical comparison to question why he has been placed under guard, as though he were a dangerous force that needed to be watched.
Did you know? Job’s question, “What is man that you should magnify him?” expresses his amazement at the great attention God gives to human beings and at His continual testing of them.
